subject: Adding a module dramatically slows down a capture-recapture model

messages.author: 7cb2eb89472f7169
messages.subject: Adding a module dramatically slows down a capture-recapture model
parts:
Hi Nimble team,

I am trying to test for an effect of food availability on survival (specifically mortality hazard rates) in a capture-recapture (CR) model. Since no clean covariate for food availability is available, I built a model to estimate food availability in each year from raw and messy data. This model on its own runs fine (~20 min), as well as the CR model on its own (~10h). But when I include the food availability module in the CR model, and include an effect of (estimated) food availability on mortality hazard rates, suddenly the model takes much longer to compile (buildMCMC() and compileNimble() steps), requires way more memory, and takes much longer to run. 

I made a test with a simulated dataset of modest size (15 years, 30 marked individuals per year, food availability data), and I confirmed that when I include both the CR module and the food module in a single model without including a parameter for an effect of food on mortality, my whole script takes ~30 mins to run. But when I include a parameter for an effect of acorn on mortality, the buildMCMC() and compileNimble() steps last ~5 minutes each instead of seconds, and the model takes >12 hours to run. With my real dataset (30 years of data, ~100 marked individuals in each year), the model becomes prohibitively slow.

Is this to be expected? Is it related to the specifics of my food availability model? Is there a way to speed things up? Any insight would be appreciated. 

The model code and the code to simulate data is attached.

Thanks in advance,

Marwan

messages.author: f116cbe5c604c988
messages.subject: Re: Adding a module dramatically slows down a capture-recapture model
parts:
Marwan, I was able to look at this.  Everything is working "fine", the issue is that when you include the acorn model, that introduces 2123 latent nodes acorn_obs[i, t, k] into the model.  Each of these must be sampled by the MCMC (and, being discrete nodes arising from a dnegbin distribution, they are all assigned slice samplers).

For each MCMC iteration, each of these 2123 acorn_obs nodes is updated.  The slice sampler which does this update requires multiple calculations of all the dependencies of each acorn_obs[i, t, k] node.  As the model is written, each of these acorn_obs[i, t, k] nodes have a total of 6672 dependencies, broken down below:

Dependencies of each acorn_obs[i, t, k] node:
first there's a single acorn_corrected[i,t,k] node - no problem here.
then a single acorn[i,t] node - no problem
then a single acorn_index[t] - no problem
then *all 15* acorn_index_s[t] nodes.

This number itself isn't a lot, but because each acorn_corrected[i,t,k] flows into *all 15* acorn_index_s[t] nodes, and in combination, all 15 acorn_index_s[t] nodes are used for mN, then in turn sW, sS, etc.... the dependencies of every individual acorn_obs[i, t, k] end up including *all* of each of the following:

acorn_index_s: 15
lik: 202
mN: 84
ones: 202
psiH: 84
psiN: 84
S: 252
sS: 84
sW: 84
zeta: 5578

for a total of 6672 dependencies.

The sampling time of these acorn_obs[i, t, k] nodes account for 99.92994 % of the total MCMC runtime.

Basically, because of this funneling of the dependencies into *all 15* of the acorn_index_s[t] nodes (because of the standardization), then fanning out from there, the dependencies of each acorn_obs node basically include most of the model.

One way to limit this would be to skip the standardization.  That is, never create acorn_index_s[t], and instead just use acorn_index[t].  I gave this a quick try, and building the MCMC took about 20% of the original time (due to so many fewer dependencies in each sampler, I believe), and the MCMC runtime itself was reduced to about 40% of the original.  So this is one option for you.

I'm sure there are other things you could do to reduce these dependencies as much as possible, but this was one quick approach, which worked pretty well.

Let me know if anything doesn't make sense.

Cheers,
Daniel

messages.author: dd632bd3bbcdd7e9
messages.subject: Re: Adding a module dramatically slows down a capture-recapture model
parts:
Hi Marwan,

I think Daniel has low availability this week so I will jump into the discussion and try to catch up.

The negbin per se is not responsible for the thick dependency structure of the model, so I wouldn't start there. (Also, if I follow, acorn_obs[i, t, k] are data, so not being sampled. Is that correct?)

If I follow, the thick dependency structure, while it inherently creates harder computation, is part of what you need. (A minor point from a comment I see is that if you need a median function, you could write one as a nimbleFunction and let us know if you need some pointers to get started.)

The main thing I would try is re-arranging things to have fewer large objects in the model. Since the number of individuals is the biggest dimension, you could try removing zeta from the model, since it has an individual index. You could do this by writing a nimbleFunction that takes as input S[1:5, 1:5, sex[i], 1:(n_occasions-1)], E[1:5, 1:5], first[i], last[i], and CH[i, 1:n_occasions] and returns lik[i]. The zeta calculations involved are all deterministic, and it would remove a huge object from the model object(s) and from the DAG (directed acyclic graph of the model) and thus potentially greatly reduce memory use.

You could also consider removing the S and E arrays and using their elements directly instead. For example, if you take the previous suggestion, you could provide p, r, sW, sS, psiH, and psiN as inputs instead of S and E. Even if you don't take the previous suggestion, you could write these inputs directly into the zeta calculations, although it appears that zeta is the really big object here, so removing S and E may not be as helpful as removing zeta.

With many thousands of individuals, if you have many duplicate capture histories, a potentially very effective trick is to include one of each and write a user-defined distribution to return the log probability you need for the duplicate set. This is illustrated in Turek et al 2016:

Turek, D., P. de Valpine, and C.J. Paciorek. 2016. Efficient Markov chain Monte Carlo sampling for hierarchical hidden Markov models. Environmental and Ecological Statistics 23:549–564. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10651-016-0353-z

If you can't get anything to work, a final idea is to make the problem sequential: estimate the acorn model and use the posterior for acorn_index_s as a prior in the CR model, for example by approximating it with a distribution.

HTH
Perry

Thanks a lot for your answer! Sorry for the delayed response, I was busy with other projects.

If I follow, the thick dependency structure, while it inherently creates harder computation, is part of what you need. (A minor point from a comment I see is that if you need a median function, you could write one as a nimbleFunction and let us know if you need some pointers to get started.)

The main thing I would try is re-arranging things to have fewer large objects in the model. Since the number of individuals is the biggest dimension, you could try removing zeta from the model, since it has an individual index. You could do this by writing a nimbleFunction that takes as input S[1:5, 1:5, sex[i], 1:(n_occasions-1)], E[1:5, 1:5], first[i], last[i], and CH[i, 1:n_occasions] and returns lik[i]. HTH

On Thursday, June 4, 2026 at 9:22:13 PM UTC+2 Daniel Turek wrote:
Marwan, I was able to look at this.  Everything is working "fine", the issue is that when you include the acorn model, that introduces 2123 latent nodes acorn_obs[i, t, k] into the model.  Each of these must be sampled by the MCMC (and, being discrete nodes arising from a dnegbin distribution, they are all assigned slice samplers).

For each MCMC iteration, each of these 2123 acorn_obs nodes is updated.  The slice sampler which does this update requires multiple calculations of all the dependencies of each acorn_obs[i, t, k] node.  As the model is written, each of these acorn_obs[i, t, k] nodes have a total of 6672 dependencies, broken down below:

Dependencies of each acorn_obs[i, t, k] node:
first there's a single acorn_corrected[i,t,k] node - no problem here.
then a single acorn[i,t] node - no problem
then a single acorn_index[t] - no problem
then *all 15* acorn_index_s[t] nodes.

This number itself isn't a lot, but because each acorn_corrected[i,t,k] flows into *all 15* acorn_index_s[t] nodes, and in combination, all 15 acorn_index_s[t] nodes are used for mN, then in turn sW, sS, etc.... the dependencies of every individual acorn_obs[i, t, k] end up including *all* of each of the following:

acorn_index_s: 15
lik: 202
mN: 84
ones: 202
psiH: 84
psiN: 84
S: 252
sS: 84
sW: 84
zeta: 5578

for a total of 6672 dependencies.

The sampling time of these acorn_obs[i, t, k] nodes account for 99.92994 % of the total MCMC runtime.

Basically, because of this funneling of the dependencies into *all 15* of the acorn_index_s[t] nodes (because of the standardization), then fanning out from there, the dependencies of each acorn_obs node basically include most of the model.

I'm sure there are other things you could do to reduce these dependencies as much as possible, but this was one quick approach, which worked pretty well.

Let me know if anything doesn't make sense.

Cheers,
Daniel

This number itself isn't a lot, but because each acorn_corrected[i,t,k] flows into *all 15* acorn_index_s[t] nodes, and in combination, all 15 acorn_index_s[t] nodes are used for mN, then in turn sW, sS, etc.... the dependencies of every individual acorn_obs[i, t, k] end up including *all* of each of the following:

acorn_index_s: 15
lik: 202
mN: 84
ones: 202
psiH: 84
psiN: 84
S: 252
sS: 84
sW: 84
zeta: 5578

for a total of 6672 dependencies.

The sampling time of these acorn_obs[i, t, k] nodes account for 99.92994 % of the total MCMC runtime.

Basically, because of this funneling of the dependencies into *all 15* of the acorn_index_s[t] nodes (because of the standardization), then fanning out from there, the dependencies of each acorn_obs node basically include most of the model.

One way to limit this would be to skip the standardization.  That is, never create acorn_index_s[t], and instead just use acorn_index[t].  I gave this a quick try, and building the MCMC took about 20% of the original time (due to so many fewer dependencies in each sampler, I believe), and the MCMC runtime itself was reduced to about 40% of the original.  So this is one option for you.

I'm sure there are other things you could do to reduce these dependencies as much as possible, but this was one quick approach, which worked pretty well.

Let me know if anything doesn't make sense.

Cheers,
Daniel
